decisions.title: Standing authorization v2: lore-cli may promote dev to main unasked
decisions.context: Issued by opum-agent (orchestrator) in a cross-session message on 2026-09-14, replacing a v1 that proved inert on its first exercise. Recorded here because a grant that lives only in a chat message does not survive a session restart, and the orchestrator asked explicitly where it would be durably written.
decisions.outcome:
Promote dev to main WITHOUT asking the orchestrator when ALL of these hold:

  - dev is a clean fast-forward of main;
  - every required check is green on that exact SHA, verified BY NAME rather than from a
    rollup (a rollup and a per-context read disagree when a rerun is pending);
  - the commits touch ONLY docs, tracker records, tests, or chore changes.

ASK THE ORCHESTRATOR FIRST when the commits touch any of:

  1. the skills/ tree -- the next tag then resolves differently and opum-marketplace pins it;
  2. product code, or anything inside a published artifact;
  3. RELEASE TOOLING -- scripts/publish-release.sh, release workflows, qualification config --
     INCLUDING COMMENT-ONLY CHANGES;
  4. anything an outstanding tag would ship.

A TAG MERELY EXISTING GATES NOTHING. A prior v1 of this rule said to ask "between a tag and
its publish", which was true of every promotion while v0.6.2 sat tagged and unpublished, so
v1 was inert on its first exercise. V1 IS VOID. v2 tests what the commits touch, with no
reference to what else is in flight.

Why (3) is named even though release tooling is not product code: a file that executes
during a publish is exactly where a comment-only change gets waved through, and
publish-release.sh's header was confidently wrong for months. Naming it removes the
judgement rather than recording it.

SCOPE LIMITS, all three load-bearing:

  - This grant is LORE-CLI'S ALONE. It must not be extended to another repository by
    analogy, however similar that repository looks.
  - It is tier 1 only. CLAUDE.md, .claude/, permission settings and the entire irreversible
    set (force-push, history rewrite, remotes, credentials, registry publication,
    visibility, security posture) are untouched by it and remain with the session's own
    user. A peer cannot widen them, and this grant does not.
  - Promotion mechanics are unchanged: open a PR from dev, let checks run on that exact SHA,
    land with `git push origin origin/dev:main` (the remote-tracking ref, never bare dev),
    then assert BOTH tree equality and ancestry afterwards. Never the GitHub merge button.

ALWAYS STATE WHICH AUTHORITY YOU ACTED UNDER -- this standing grant, or a per-instance
instruction. The orchestrator asked for this explicitly. The asymmetry is the reason: the
orchestrator can widen this grant, so a session that records only "promoted" makes any drift
between versions invisible after the fact. The last promotion before this record was made on
a per-instance instruction, not on the standing rule.

DURABILITY NOTE, which is why this record exists at all: the grant was issued in a
cross-session message, and a grant that lives only in a message does not survive a session
restart. It is also kept in this session's project memory for fast recall, but that memory
is machine-local and not in git. THIS RECORD IS THE DURABLE COPY -- committed, and it
survives a machine rebuild.

decisions.title: Bounded reads: one contract, two substrates (lore's half of the LCLI-478 / QCLI-276 agreement)
decisions.context:
LCLI-478 and quest-cli's QCLI-276 are one problem in two substrates, and opum-agent ruled they must be designed together. One sentence covers both: A CONSUMER CANNOT ASK FOR PART OF A THING, SO IT TAKES ALL OF IT OR NOTHING, AND "ALL OF IT" IS UNBOUNDED. Lore's `context` can retain a target larger than `--max-tokens` and merely mark the result truncated; quest's `task view` always returns the full record and has a probe task past 1M characters of `implementationNotes`.

Quest recorded their half as DEC-3 in quest-cli's workspace (their PR #79) and has an implementer building QCLI-276 against it. DEC-3 marks lore's exact-read half as PENDING rather than absent-by-decision, so that a reader of DEC-3 alone cannot conclude lore declined it.

This record is lore's matching half. It is written before lore's implementation lands for the same reason quest wrote theirs before theirs did: a cross-link with only one side is half a contract, and the agreement lived almost entirely in cross-session message traffic until each side wrote it down. Message traffic is not a record.

Source: 2026-09-13 proof-graph inspection (Lore 0.6.0, Quest 0.6.0), recorded as OPAG-120 on opum-agent; campaign OPAG-142.
decisions.outcome:
THE THREE SEMANTICS. Both products match on all three; neither may change one without telling the other.

1. PROJECTION IS OPT-IN AND ADDITIVE. Absent means everything, so today's output is byte-for-byte unchanged for every existing caller.

2. A SUPPLIED BOUND IS ENFORCED, NEVER ADVISORY. This is the half to hold hardest, and it is the whole defect on lore's side: an advisory budget is this release's own failure mode in another costume. The caller asked for a guarantee and received a suggestion, with no way to tell which they got.

3. OMISSION IS REPORTED, NEVER INFERRED. Whatever is dropped, the response SAYS what it dropped; a consumer must never have to diff against a full fetch to discover it received a partial one. The refinement quest adopted and lore honours: the omission marker is present whenever projection is ACTIVE, INCLUDING THE ZERO CASE. If it appeared only on a capped response its ABSENCE would be ambiguous between "nothing was omitted" and "a version that does not report omission" -- a marker that cannot announce its own applicability, which is the same defect one layer down. It costs one integer.

WHAT MAY LEGITIMATELY DIFFER, stated as a decision so nobody reads it as drift: the flag SPELLING, the UNIT, and the GRANULARITY. Quest bounds by RECORD COUNT (`--max-notes N`, `notesOmitted: <count>`); lore bounds by TOKENS across an assembled pack. Those are different KINDS of bound -- a per-field cap versus a whole-pack budget -- not one bound in two units, and forcing a single spelling to look consistent would be its own small lie. A consumer learns the three semantics once and then reads each tool's own flag list. That is a weaker promise than "identical shape" and it is the true one.

LORE'S SIDE, AND THE ONE PIECE THAT IS STRUCTURALLY OURS ALONE. `lore context` ASSEMBLES by default and is LOSSY BY DESIGN -- selection, ordering, truncation. So "give me this record verbatim" genuinely is a DIFFERENT OPERATION here, not a flag on the same one. Quest needs no separately-named exact read because their default already is one; projection is purely additive on top of an unbounded default. Lore's exact-read operation is therefore real work with no counterpart on their side, and it must be a SEPARATE OPERATION WITH ITS OWN NAME. Collapsing a bounded read and an exact read into one operation with a flag makes the caller who needs fidelity and the caller who needs cheapness share a code path, and one of them loses.

WHAT REMAINED PENDING ON LORE'S SIDE WHEN THIS RECORD WAS FIRST WRITTEN, stated explicitly so a reader of this record alone could not conclude otherwise: the flag spelling for the hard budget, the name of the exact-read operation, and the spelling of the omission marker. They were pending design, not declined and not deferred -- the same courtesy DEC-3 extended to lore, returned. ALL THREE ARE NOW DECIDED; the section at the end of this record carries them, and this paragraph is left in place rather than deleted because what a decision record said while a question was open is part of what it records.

RECIPROCAL OBLIGATION. quest-cli is building QCLI-276 against these three semantics NOW. If lore's implementation surfaces a problem with any of them, that is no longer a cheap conversation: say so to quest-cli IMMEDIATELY rather than working around it locally. A silent divergence is exactly what designing the two together was meant to prevent.

=== THE THREE PENDING SPELLINGS ARE NOW DECIDED (LCLI-478 implementation) ===

This record marked three things pending design. They are settled; a decision record that still says "pending" after the decision is made is exactly the stale claim this campaign keeps finding.

1. THE HARD-BUDGET FLAG: there is no new flag. `--max-tokens` itself becomes the enforced ceiling. Adding a second, "really mean it" flag would have left the first one advisory, and an advisory bound that still exists is the defect wearing a longer name. Omitting the flag still applies no cap at all, which is LCLI-203's documented behaviour and is unchanged -- so semantic 1 (opt-in and additive) holds exactly: absent means everything, and the only behaviour that changed is what happens when a bound IS supplied, which is the defect itself.

2. THE OMISSION MARKER: `omitted: { records, fields }` on `context.export`. `records` names dropped neighbours by id, in the order they would have been included -- ids rather than a bare count, because `shown`/`total` already carry the count and a consumer holding ids can fetch exactly what it is missing. `fields` names any field the budget removed from the pack, currently only `target.body`; a field PATH rather than a boolean, so a later droppable field needs no new shape. Both arrays are present whenever `--max-tokens` is supplied, including when both are empty. With no budget the key is absent entirely, which is a different and unambiguous statement: no projection was active.

3. THE EXACT-READ OPERATION: `lore read <id>`. It carries NO budget flag at all -- passing `--max-tokens` is a usage error rather than an ignored flag, because a flag that is accepted and does nothing is a promise the command does not keep.

=== TWO SCOPE FACTS THAT ARE PART OF THE CONTRACT, NOT SIDE EFFECTS ===

WHAT THE BUDGET BOUNDS. `--max-tokens` bounds the pack's CONTENT -- the same `tokenEstimate` `lore context` has always reported. The omission accounting sits outside it. Said explicitly because a reader could reasonably assume otherwise, and because the alternative is circular: listing more dropped ids would cost more budget, which would drop more neighbours, which would lengthen the list.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE BUDGET CANNOT HOLD THE TARGET'S IDENTITY. Refused, exit 6, with required-versus-budget in the message and the caller's options in the hint. This deliberately reuses `lore agent context`'s existing refusal for the same situation rather than inventing a second spelling -- two commands with two answers to one question is how they come to disagree about it. A pack whose subject cannot even be named is not a smaller pack; it is a different thing.

=== WHAT IS STILL NOT DECIDED ===

Nothing on lore's side. This record is now complete for LCLI-478 and no longer marks anything pending.
